caption:
Who built Great Zimbabwe?

Ancestors of the Shona people. Stone building began in the 11th century and continued for over 300 years. The Great Enclosure's dry-stone walls stand up to 11 m high and run about 250 m — no mortar anywhere in them. Gold, ivory, Chinese porcelain and Arabian coins passed through the city.

In 1871 the German geographer Karl Mauch was shown the ruins and immediately discounted African construction, favouring a legend that they copied the Queen of Sheba's palace. He claimed a wooden lintel must be Lebanese cedar. Looters followed: W.G. Neal's Ancient Ruins Company stripped the site of anything sellable between the 1890s and 1920s and destroyed what it could not carry.

David Randall-MacIver in 1905–06 and Gertrude Caton Thompson in 1929 both concluded the site was medieval and Bantu. African origin only became consensus in the 1950s, and Rhodesia kept pushing back. The archaeologist Paul Sinclair recalled being told it was acceptable to say "yellow people" built it, but that he could not mention radiocarbon dates; a board trustee threatened his job if he said publicly that black Africans built Zimbabwe.

Still unresolved: why the city emptied in the 16th or 17th century. Shona oral tradition blames a salt shortage. And the Conical Tower cannot be dated — Bent dug into it without training in the 1890s and destroyed the stratigraphy.

Images: CDC/Dr J. Lyle Conrad, 1975; Jan Derk, 1997; Smart & Copley, c.1890–1925; J. Theodore Bent, 1892; Karl Mauch's own notes; a wood engraving from Die Gartenlaube, 1896. All public domain.
